pr_title: Add support for DEC macro operations
pr_body:
## Summary of the Pull Request

This PR adds support for the DEC macro operations `DECDMAC` (Define Macro), and `DECINVM` (Invoke Macro), which allow an application to define a sequence of characters as a macro, and then later invoke that macro to execute the content as if it had just been received from the host.

This PR also adds two new `DSR` queries: one for reporting the available space remaining in the macro buffer (`DECMSR`), and another reporting a checksum of the macros that are currently defined (`DECCKSR`).

## PR Checklist
* [x] Closes #14205
* [x] CLA signed.
* [x] Tests added/passed
* [ ] Documentation updated.
* [ ] Schema updated.
* [ ] I've discussed this with core contributors already. If not checked, I'm ready to accept this work might be rejected in favor of a different grand plan. Issue number where discussion took place: #xxx

## Detailed Description of the Pull Request / Additional comments

I've created a separate `MacroBuffer` class to handle the parsing and storage of macros, so the `AdaptDispatch` class doesn't have to do much more than delegate the macro operations to that.

The one complication is the macro invocation, which requires injecting characters back into the state machine's input stream. Ideally we'd just pass the content to the `ProcessString` method, but we can't do that when it's already in the middle of a `CSI` dispatch.

My solution for this was to add an `OnCsiComplete` method via which we could register a callback function that injects the macro sequence only once the state machine has returned to the ground state. This feels a bit hacky, but that was the best approach I could come up with.

## Validation Steps Performed

Thanks to @KalleOlaviNiemitalo, we've been able to do some testing on a real VT420 to determine how the macro operations are intended to work, and I've tried to get our implementation to match that behavior as much as possible (we differ in some aspects of the checksum reporting, where the VT420 behavior seemed undesirable, or potentially buggy).

I've also added unit tests covering some of the same scenarios that we tested on the VT420.

issue_context.title: Add support for the VT macro operations
issue_context.body:
# Description of the new feature/enhancement

There are a couple of operations that were introduced on the VT420 that allow an application to define a sequence of a characters as a macro ([`DECDMAC`](https://vt100.net/docs/vt510-rm/DECDMAC.html)), and then later invoke that macro to execute the content as if it had just been received from the host ([`DECINVM`](https://vt100.net/docs/vt510-rm/DECINVM.html)).

This can be a useful optimization in gaming if you need to define a sprite made up of a number of characters, spanning multiple rows, and using multiple colors. If you can upload the sequences for drawing the sprite as a macro, then any time you need to render it, you just set the cursor position and invoke it.

There is a similar use case for sound effects that need to be played more than once. Instead of having to upload a long set of `DECPS` sequences every time you play the sound, you just invoke a macro which has been predefined with the necessary sequences.

# Proposed technical implementation details (optional)

The one complication is how we get the macro content injected into the output stream when it's invoked. The way I'm handling that in my current POC is with a kind of callback function that can be registered with the state machine, and which gets executed (if set) once we return to the ground state from a `CSI` action.

So in the dispatch handler for `DECINVM`, we register a lambda callback with the state machine which then injects the additional macro content with a `ProcessString` call once the state machine has returned to ground. It's a little more complicated than that, because the `ProcessString` implementation isn't reentrant, so we also need to save some state, but that's the basic gist of it.

I don't know if there's a nicer way of handling this, but that's my current plan if you're happy to accept a PR for this.
comments: Wouldn't it be possible to `.replace()` the macro in the input buffer with the replacement string?

> Wouldn't it be possible to `.replace()` the macro in the input buffer with the replacement string?

Not easily, no. The state machine is designed to work with an immutable `wstring_view` so I suspect that would require a significant rewrite. It could also be quiet inefficient when dealing with large macros, and/or nested macro invocations - you'd be allocating a bunch of additional memory for content that you already have in an existing string. Ideally we just want to pass that string directly to the state machine as is.
@j4james, do we need to test what VT420 does with recursive macros?
@KalleOlaviNiemitalo Yeah, there are actually quite a few aspects of the macros handling I'd like to check. I'm still putting together the test cases though.

@KalleOlaviNiemitalo I've put together my first set of tests [here](https://gist.github.com/j4james/1210babd182ad5f471647b7c94a1686f). I've grouped them all on a single page so you don't have to do hundreds of screenshots this time. But as always there's no rush for this - just whenever you have a chance.

I'm also hoping to put together another set of tests covering the macro DSR operations (reporting the available memory, and checksums of the defined macros), but it'll take me a while longer to get to that.

In case it help, this is my best guess of what the output should look like:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4181424/198359655-f325c352-a99e-4418-b5b9-3c38ebfc2e37.png)
Are there applications that use the macro feature? How do they detect whether the terminal supports macros? IIRC terminfo does not define capabilities for that.

> Are there applications that use the macro feature?

I was mostly doing this for use in my own applications, so I haven't really looked to see if anyone else is using macros. But I do know that libsixel is supposed to use them in some way to optimize gif animations. I haven't tested that with my sixel branch, because it's too far diverged to merge with anything recent, but I suspect we'd need to extend the permitted macro size quite a lot if we want that to work, and I'm not sure that's a good idea. But we can worry about that if/when we get sixel support.

> How do they detect whether the terminal supports macros?

It's extension number 32 in the `DA` report, but it's a required feature for level 4 and above, so assumedly your VT420 wouldn't report that. Unfortunately modern terminal emulators tend to lie about their conformance level, so you can't really rely on that. Best bet may be to define a macro that triggers something like a `DA` report, execute that macro, and then see whether you get anything aback.

But ignoring everyone else, we will need to update our own `DA` response at some point to include this extension, and possibly a few other features that have been added recently (e.g. the rectangular area operations, and soft fonts). I've been putting that off because I'm not exactly sure how we're going to make that work over conpty.

review_comments: Doesn't that mean that the checksum won't match the output expected by such applications anyways then?

What I'm saying is that nobody is likely to depend on that behavior because it's nondeterministic. As long as they do a full delete when uploading their macros, we should match the expected checksum. And if they aren't doing a full delete, they shouldn't be using a checksum, because the results would be unpredictable. If I'm wrong about that, we can always revisit this implementation.
I may be wrong, but I was under the impression that that wouldn't actually free up the memory.

No that should for sure work. `.clear()` doesn't free memory, but in this case `{}` will construct a brand new instance of `std::wstring` and then move-assign it to `macro`, whose contents will be entirely replaced by the new instance.

I've just tried this now and that doesn't seem to be the case. I created a 200K macro, and then deleted it, logging `macro.capacity()` before and after the delete. With the `macro = {}` the capacity remained at 200K. With `std::wstring{}.swap(macro)`, it shrunk down to 7 (I'm assuming that's the default). That suggested to me that `macro = {}` is not actually freeing the memory. Or have I misunderstood the meaning of `capacity`?

Welp, I didn't expect that either: https://godbolt.org/z/PMMq85cE7
It's because `std::basic_string` got a
```cpp
constexpr basic_string& operator=(std::initializer_list<CharT> ilist);
```

So anyways, C++ is a simple language, that's easy to understand... /s 😑
